Recorded 13 February 2017}} }} '''Andrew Murray Burnham'''{{efn|{{IPAc-en|ˈ|b|ɜɹ|n|ə|m|audio=Andrew Murray Burnham pronunciation.wav}}}} (born 7 January 1970) is a British politician who has served as [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom]] and [[Leader of the Labour Party (UK)|Leader of the Labour Party]] since July 2026. He has been [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) for [[Makerfield (constituency)|Makerfield]] in [[Greater Manchester]] since June 2026, and was [[Mayor of Greater Manchester]] from 2017 to 2026; before that he was MP for [[Leigh (constituency)|Leigh]] from 2001 to 2017 and held several [[Cabinet of the United Kingdom|Cabinet]] positions. Burnham identifies as a [[socialist]] and is associated with the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]]'s [[soft left]]; he is also a member of the [[Co-operative Party]], which is [[Labour and Co-operative Party|allied with Labour]]. His political ideology has been called "[[Manchesterism]]". Burnham was born and brought up in [[northern England]]. He joined Labour at the age of 15 and read English at [[Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge]]. He worked as a journalist and [[Special adviser (United Kingdom)|political adviser]] before being elected the MP for Leigh [[2001 United Kingdom general election|in 2001]]. Under the prime ministers [[Tony Blair]] and [[Gordon Brown]], he was [[Chief Secretary to the Treasury]] and [[Culture Secretary]], in which capacity he launched the [[Hillsborough Independent Panel]]. In 2009 he was promoted to [[Secretary of State for Health and Social Care|Health Secretary]]; he responded to the [[swine flu pandemic]] and launched an independent inquiry into the [[Stafford Hospital scandal]]. After Labour's defeat at the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]], Burnham served in the [[shadow cabinet]] from 2010 to 2016. He stood for the Labour leadership [[2010 Labour Party leadership election (UK)|in 2010]] and [[2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)|in 2015]], coming fourth and second respectively. In 2017 he stood down as an MP and [[2017 Greater Manchester mayoral election|was elected]] Mayor of Greater Manchester. He reorganised Manchester's [[Manchester Metrolink|tram]] and [[Buses in Manchester|bus]] systems as the [[Bee Network]] and received the nickname "King of the North" for campaigning for more [[Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme|furlough funding]] for Northern communities during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom|COVID-19 pandemic]]. Burnham's tenure as mayor increased his national profile and he was re-elected [[2021 Greater Manchester mayoral election|in 2021]] and [[2024 Greater Manchester mayoral election|in 2024]]. Following Labour's [[2024 United Kingdom general election|return to government in 2024]], Burnham maintained strong approval ratings as those of the prime minister, [[Keir Starmer]], [[2026 Labour Party leadership crisis|declined]], and came to be seen as a potential successor. He returned to Parliament in 2026 by winning the [[2026 Makerfield by-election|Makerfield by-election]] and [[2026 Greater Manchester mayoral by-election|resigned as mayor]]. Starmer announced his resignation, leading to [[2026 Labour Party leadership election|a party leadership election]] which Burnham won unopposed. During [[Premiership of Andy Burnham|his premiership]], Burnham has announced policies to move some government administration out of London as [[No. 10 North]], cut fares on [[Bus transport in the United Kingdom|buses]], reduce business rates on [[pub]]s, increase government support for [[Apprenticeships in the United Kingdom|apprenticeships]], establish a [[National Care Service]], and continue [[Ukraine–United Kingdom relations|support for Ukraine]]. ==Early life and education== {{Andy Burnham sidebar}} Andrew Murray Burnham was born on 7 January 1970 in [[Aintree, Lancashire]], England,{{Efn|name=Aintree|Formerly in Lancashire, Aintree has been in [[Merseyside]] since the county's creation in 1974.}} a suburb of [[Liverpool]], and was brought up in [[Culcheth]].{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-33520320|title=Who is Andy Burnham? Labour leadership contender guide|work=BBC News|date=30 July 2015|archive-date=3 July 2026|access-date=13 January 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260703142426/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-33520320|url-status=live}}{{Who's Who|author=|title=Burnham, Rt Hon. There he earned the [[nickname]] "Seven Eights", because of his "inability to remember that seven eights are 56" when reciting his [[Multiplication table|times tables]].{{cite news|url=https://www.goodhousekeeping.com/uk/lifestyle/a73200936/andy-burnham-school-nickname/|title='They called our Andy "Seven Eights"': Andy Burnham's school nickname & what it means - according to his mum|last=Jenkins|first=Bethan Rose|date=21 July 2026|work=[[Good Housekeeping]]|access-date=24 July 2026}} Burnham was raised Catholic, and served as an [[Altar server|altar boy]] at his local church. He later described himself as "Catholic by upbringing" but "not particularly religious". He said: "[[Catholic social teaching]] underpins my politics. We did have to read the [[Catechism of the Catholic Church|catechism]] at school but it is powerful and strong and right."{{cite news|title=Andy Burnham Interview: Part 2|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.co.uk/2015/08/10/andy-burnham-interview-catholic-church-tampon-tax_n_7961096.html|access-date=27 April 2025|work=HuffPost UK|date=10 August 2015|language=en|archive-date=23 May 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250523080214/https://www.huffingtonpost.co.uk/2015/08/10/andy-burnham-interview-catholic-church-tampon-tax_n_7961096.html|url-status=live}} He joined the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] when he was 15.{{cite web|title=Orders of the Day — European Communities (Amendment) Bill|url=https://www.theyworkforyou.com/debates/?id=2001-07-04.333.1|website=They Work For You|access-date=7 November 2021|archive-date=7 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211107215425/https://www.theyworkforyou.com/debates/?id=2001-07-04.333.1|url-status=live}} Burnham read English at the [[University of Cambridge]], where he was an undergraduate at [[Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge|Fitzwilliam College]]. He received an [[British undergraduate degree classification|upper second-class]] [[Bachelor of Arts]] (BA) degree.{{Cite web|last=Collins|first=David|date=23 May 2026|title=Who is Andy Burnham really? Teen 'scally' to professional outsider|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/andy-burnham-manchester-labour-makerfield-by-election-jq80trkk8|url-access=subscription|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260525015801/https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/andy-burnham-manchester-labour-makerfield-by-election-jq80trkk8|archive-date=25 May 2026|access-date=31 May 2026|website=The Times|language=en-GB}} As per tradition, his BA was later promoted to a [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge and Dublin)|Master of Arts]] (MA Cantab) degree.{{cite web|publisher=Webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk|url=http://www.dh.gov.uk/en/Aboutus/MinistersandDepartmentLeaders/Ministers/Ministersbiography/DH_100325|archive-url=http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20100407204138/www.dh.gov.uk/en/Aboutus/MinistersandDepartmentLeaders/Ministers/Ministersbiography/DH_100325|url-status=dead|archive-date=7 April 2010|title=Biography of Andy Burnham : Department of Health|access-date=9 April 2013}} ==Early political career== After university, Burnham moved to London. From 1991 to 1994 he was a journalist for a private company, Baltic Publishing, assigned to their [[trade magazine]] ''Tank Container World'' (later ''Bulk Distributor''), a magazine covering [[Tank truck|tanker]] and [[Intermodal freight transport|intermodal transportation]].{{cite web | last=Chambers | first=Sam | title=Former logistics reporter set to become Britain's latest prime minister | website=Splash247 | date=16 July 2026 | url=https://splash247.com/former-logistics-reporter-set-to-become-britains-latest-prime-minister/?utm_source=dlvr.it&utm_medium=linkedin | access-date=16 July 2026}}{{cite news |last1=O'Neill |first1=Sean |title=Andy Burnham's story of an oh-so-changeable ambassador for change |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/who-is-andy-burnham-manchester-mayor-makerfield-c5j9nhg0n |work=The Times |date=17 June 2026 |archive-date=23 June 2026 |access-date=22 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260623105753/https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/who-is-andy-burnham-manchester-mayor-makerfield-c5j9nhg0n |url-status=live }}{{cite news |title=Former BD journalist set to become UK PM |url=https://bulk-distributor.com/2026/07/former-bd-journalist-set-to-become-uk-pm/ |access-date=10 July 2026 |work=Bulk Distributor |archive-date=14 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260714005801/https://bulk-distributor.com/2026/07/former-bd-journalist-set-to-become-uk-pm/ |url-status=live }}{{cite news |title=BD turns 30 |url=https://bulk-distributor.com/2020/03/17042/ |access-date=10 July 2026 |work=Bulk Distributor |archive-date=13 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260713052245/https://bulk-distributor.com/2020/03/17042/ |url-status=live }} From 1994 until the [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997 general election]] he was a researcher for [[Tessa Jowell]]. He joined the [[Transport and General Workers' Union]] in 1995. Following the 1997 election, he was a parliamentary officer for the [[NHS Confederation]] from August to December 1997, before taking up the post as an administrator with the Football Task Force for a year.{{cite news|title=New culture secretary keeps an open mind on licence fee|work=[[The Guardian]]|last=Woodward|first=Will|date=26 January 2008|url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2008/jan/26/uk.media|publisher=[[Guardian News & Media]]|access-date=12 October 2008|location=London|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081005143739/http://www.guardian.co.uk/politics/2008/jan/26/uk.media|archive-date=5 October 2008|url-status=live}} In 1998, he became a [[Special adviser (United Kingdom)|special adviser]] to the [[Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport]], [[Chris Smith, Baron Smith of Finsbury|Chris Smith]], a position he held until he was elected to the House of Commons in the [[2001 United Kingdom general election|2001 general election]]. === Member of Parliament (2001–2017) === Following the retirement of [[Lawrence Cunliffe]], Burnham successfully applied to be the parliamentary candidate for [[Leigh (constituency)|Leigh]] in Greater Manchester, then a Labour [[safe seat]]. At the 2001 election he was elected with a majority of 16,362, and gave his [[maiden speech]] in the House of Commons on 4 July 2001.{{cite web|date=4 July 2001|access-date=12 October 2008|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200102/cmhansrd/vo010704/debtext/10704-21.htm#10704-21_spnew1|title=House of Commons Hansard; vol 371, part 14, col 333|work=[[Hansard]]|publisher=[[Parliament of the United Kingdom]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630013226/http://www.publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200102/cmhansrd/vo010704/debtext/10704-21.htm#10704-21_spnew1|archive-date=30 June 2009|url-status=live}} Following his election to Parliament, Burnham was a member of the [[Health Select Committee]] from 2001 until 2003, when he was appointed [[Parliamentary private secretary]] (PPS) to the [[Home Secretary]] [[David Blunkett]]. Following Blunkett's first resignation in 2004, he became PPS to the [[Secretary of State for Education|education secretary]] [[Ruth Kelly]]. As well as Labour, Burnham is a member of the [[Co-operative Party]], which has been [[Labour and Co-operative Party|allied to Labour]] since 1927 and runs all candidates jointly with it.{{cite web |title=FAQ: Labour and the Co-operative Party |url=https://party.coop/about/faq-labour-and-the-co-operative-party/ |publisher=[[Co-operative Party]] |access-date=29 June 2026}}{{cite web |title=How the quietly radical Co-op Party is a driving force behind Labour's plans for power |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/independentpremium/politics-explained/labour-coop-rayner-starmer-b2628497.html |work=[[The Independent]] |date=13 October 2024 |access-date=29 June 2026}}{{cite web |title=Co-operation and collaboration at the heart of Burnham's economic plan |url=https://www.thenews.coop/co-operation-and-collaboration-at-the-heart-of-burnhams-economic-plan/ |website=[[Co-op News]] |publisher=[[Co-operative Press]] |access-date=29 June 2026}} ===Frontbench roles (2005–2010)=== ==== 2005–2007: Early ministerial career ==== Following the [[2005 United Kingdom general election|2005 general election]], Burnham was promoted to serve in Tony Blair's government as Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, where he was responsible for implementing the Identity Cards Act 2006. In the government reshuffle on 5 May 2006, he left the Home Office to become Minister of State for Delivery and Reform at the Department of Health.{{Cite web|title=Department of Health Departmental Report 2007|url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/243293/7093.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=15 July 2021|archive-date=18 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211018092236/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/243293/7093.pdf}} When Gordon Brown formed his first cabinet on 28 June 2007, Burnham was appointed Chief Secretary to the Treasury, a position he held until 2008. for society as a whole." He added, "My job – Government's job – is to preserve the value in the system."{{Cite web|url=http://www.ukmusic.org/events/122-andy-burnham-and-charlie-mccreevy-speak-at-uk-musics-first-creators-conference|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100716015417/http://www.ukmusic.org/events/122-andy-burnham-and-charlie-mccreevy-speak-at-uk-musics-first-creators-conference|url-status=dead|title=Andy Burnham and Charlie McCreevy speak at UK Music's first creators' conference|archive-date=16 July 2010}} In April 2009, after being heckled by the crowd at the 20th anniversary memorial of the Hillsborough disaster, Burnham raised the issue at the next day's cabinet meeting in Downing Street. He requested permission from Gordon Brown to raise the disaster in Parliament, and Brown agreed. This intervention ultimately led to the establishment of the second Hillsborough inquiry. By 2014, when Burnham spoke at the 25th anniversary of the disaster, his pivotal role was recognized as he was cheered and applauded by the crowd.{{cite news|first=Mike|last=McCarthy|url=http://news.sky.com/story/1243046/liverpool-remembers-hillsborough-disaster|title=Liverpool Remembers Hillsborough Disaster|publisher=British Sky Broadcasting|work=Sky News|date=15 April 2014|access-date=1 May 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429163859/http://news.sky.com/story/1243046/liverpool-remembers-hillsborough-disaster|archive-date=29 April 2016}} On 27 April 2016, the day after the Hillsborough inquest verdict that found the 96 Hillsborough deaths had occurred as a result of [[unlawful killing]], Burnham made a speech to the House of Commons calling for those responsible to be held to account. Condemning [[South Yorkshire Police]], which had instigated a cover-up in the aftermath of the tragedy, he described the force as being "rotten to the core" while suggesting that the cover-up had been "advanced in the committee rooms of this House and in the press rooms of 10 Downing Street". The eleven-minute statement drew applause from MPs, a response that is generally against convention at Westminster.{{cite news |first=Andrew |last=Stuart |url=http://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/andy-burnhams-11-minute-speech-11252538 |title=Andy Burnham's 11-minute speech on Hillsborough that left the Commons silent – and drew a round of applause |publisher=Trinity Mirror |newspaper=Manchester Evening News |date=27 April 2016 |access-date=1 May 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160501160139/http://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/andy-burnhams-11-minute-speech-11252538 |archive-date=1 May 2016}}{{cite news |first=Charlie |last=Cooper |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/hillsborough-verdict-andy-burnham-demands-south-yorkshire-police-chief-resigns-in-extraordinary-a7003536.html |title=Hillsborough verdict: Andy Burnham demands South Yorkshire police chief resigns in extraordinary speech |publisher=Independent Print Limited |newspaper=The Independent |date=27 April 2016 |access-date=1 May 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160430031741/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/hillsborough-verdict-andy-burnham-demands-south-yorkshire-police-chief-resigns-in-extraordinary-a7003536.html |archive-date=30 April 2016}} This campaign reached a historic milestone in July 2026 when the House of Commons passed the Public Office (Accountability) Bill, widely known as the Hillsborough Law. Pushed through by the departing [[Keir Starmer]] [[Starmer ministry|government]], the legislation establishes a statutory duty of candour for public officials and ensures non-means-tested legal aid for families facing the state at inquests. Burnham hailed the bill's passage as a fundamental "rewiring of the state" that would finally dismantle institutional cover-up culture, completing a personal full-circle political journey just days before he took office as Prime Minister.{{Cite news |last=Elgot |first=Jessica |last2=Conn |first2=David |date=2026-07-14 |title=Burnham hails Hillsborough law as 'rewiring of the state' as MPs approve bill |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/14/burnham-hails-hillsborough-law-rewiring-state-mps-approve-bill |access-date=2026-07-24 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} ==== 2009–2010: Health Secretary and the Stafford Hospital inquiry ==== [[File:Andy Burnham (cropped).jpg|right|thumb|235x235px|Official portrait as Health Secretary, 2009]]In June 2009, Burnham was promoted to Secretary of State for Health, a post he held until the Labour government resigned following the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]]. In July 2009, just a month after taking office, he launched an independent inquiry chaired by Robert Francis QC into [[Stafford Hospital scandal|unusually high mortality rates at Stafford Hospital]] (later renamed [[County Hospital, Stafford|County Hospital]]).{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/staffordshire/8160385.stm|title=Fresh inquiry at failing hospital|work=BBC News|date=21 July 2009|access-date=25 August 2015|archive-date=14 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211214042425/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/staffordshire/8160385.stm|url-status=live}} The inquiry uncovered systematic failures and heavily criticized the care provided by the Mid Staffordshire NHS Foundation Trust.{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2010/feb/24/mid-staffordshire-hospital-inquiry|title=Mid Staffordshire NHS trust left patients humiliated and in pain |author=Sarah Boseley |newspaper=The Guardian |date=24 February 2010 |access-date=25 August 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151019004601/http://www.theguardian.com/society/2010/feb/24/mid-staffordshire-hospital-inquiry |archive-date=19 October 2015}}{{cite book|url=http://www.dh.gov.uk/en/Publicationsandstatistics/Publications/PublicationsPolicyAndGuidance/DH_113018|title=Robert Francis Inquiry report into Mid-Staffordshire NHS Foundation Trust|author=Robert Francis QC|publisher=House of Commons|date=24 February 2010|isbn=978-0-10-296439-4|access-date=24 February 2010|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605015905/http://www.dh.gov.uk/en/Publicationsandstatistics/Publications/PublicationsPolicyAndGuidance/DH_113018|archive-date=5 June 2011}} A subsequent, wider public inquiry—also led by Francis—was launched in 2010 by Burnham's Conservative successor, [[Andrew Lansley]]. resulted in major cabinet changes, featuring a significant removal of close Starmer allies, while returning and rewarding those contributing to his downfall. Key departures from the [[Starmer ministry|previous ministry]] included [[Rachel Reeves]], who was removed as Chancellor after reportedly turning down an alternative role; [[David Lammy]], who was dismissed as Deputy Prime Minister and Justice Secretary; Business Secretary [[Peter Kyle]]; Housing Secretary [[Steve Reed (politician)|Steve Reed]]; Attorney General [[Richard Hermer, Baron Hermer|Lord Hermer]]; Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and Minister for Intergovernmental Affairs [[Darren Jones]]; and Science, Innovation and Technology Secretary [[Liz Kendall]], whose department was dissolved. 15 were dismissed from the cabinet, the most in a transition within the same party since [[First Johnson ministry|Boris Johnson's first cabinet]].{{Cite news |date=2026-07-22|title=electionmapsuk (@electionmapsuk) on X|url=https://x.com/electionmapsuk/status/2080051635984687253|access-date=2026-07-23|work=X (formerly Twitter)|language=en-US}} Following the major dismissals, Burnham began selecting the senior members of his government, making many high-profile appointments and retentions. [[John Healey]] made a surprise return to government as Chancellor of the Exchequer, while [[Ed Miliband]] was elevated to Foreign Secretary, a major step up from his former Energy and Net Zero brief. Close ally [[Louise Haigh]] was appointed First Secretary of State, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and Minister for the Cabinet Office (his ''de facto'' Deputy Prime Minister). [[Angela Rayner]] returned to government in her previous post of Housing Secretary, [[Yvette Cooper]] was reshuffled to become Health Secretary and [[Wes Streeting]] re-joined the cabinet with his appointment as Defence Secretary. Rounding out the senior team, [[Jonathan Reynolds]] was promoted to the newly expanded brief of Business, Science, Innovation and Trade Secretary, while Labour Deputy Leader [[Lucy Powell]] became Education Secretary, and [[Emma Reynolds]] returned to the Treasury, being appointed as Chief Secretary to the Treasury. Some notable retentions from Starmer's cabinet included [[Shabana Mahmood]] as Home Secretary, [[Pat McFadden]] as Work and Pensions Secretary, [[Alan Campbell (politician)|Alan Campbell]] as Leader of the Commons, [[Lisa Nandy]] as Culture Secretary, and [[Heidi Alexander]] as Transport Secretary. Burnham's cabinet is the first in history with a majority of female ministerial appointments, with 12 of the 23{{nbsp}}members of the cabinet (which includes the Prime Minister) being women. He criticised the "rage rhetoric and haste" driven by the Blair and Bush administrations, while highlighting the catastrophic absence of a viable post-war stabilisation plan.{{Cite news|last=Timan|first=Joseph|date=10 March 2024|title=Five things we learned about Andy Burnham from his new book|url=https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/five-things-learned-andy-burnham-28776663|access-date=18 May 2026|work=[[Manchester Evening News]]|archive-date=3 June 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260603060852/https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/five-things-learned-andy-burnham-28776663|url-status=live}}{{better source needed|reason=tabloid|date=July 2026}} ==== United States ==== Burnham's stance on the United States mixes political criticism with practical diplomacy. His economic and trade strategy takes cues from [[Joe Biden]]'s policies on manufacturing and workers' rights. He also has long-standing ties to US Democrats; his Director of Political Strategy, Matthew McGregor, worked on [[Barack Obama]]'s [[Barack Obama 2012 presidential campaign|2012 campaign]]. By contrast, Burnham has been highly critical of [[Donald Trump]], once urging UK voters to reject the "divided, dark politics" seen in America.{{Cite web |title=PM call with President Trump of the United States: 20 July 2026 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/pm-call-with-president-trump-of-the-united-states-20-july-2026 |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}} Since becoming Prime Minister, Burnham has tried to build a working relationship with the Trump administration. In their first phone call, Burnham pointed to his plan to raise UK defence spending to 3.5% of GDP and his decision to let US forces use British bases for strikes against Iran. Trump's public response to Burnham has shifted over time. He initially dismissed Burnham as "the mayor of a town" and "extremely liberal", but later praised Burnham's North Sea oil policies, saying they would make the UK "one of the richest countries anywhere." Tensions remain, however, because Burnham appointed Ed Miliband—a vocal Trump critic—as Foreign Secretary, which angered White House officials.{{Cite web |date=2026-07-20 |title=Trump and Burnham: Can the two leaders work together? |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cqx78j77ej2o |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}} ====NATO==== In 2015, Burnham drew a hard line on national security during the Labour leadership race, warning that he would quit the Shadow Cabinet if the party ever backed leaving [[NATO]]. This was a direct challenge to Corbyn, who had questioned the military alliance and suggesting Britain should withdraw. Burnham's ultimatum put the spotlight on a massive ideological rift within Labour, forcing a tense debate over the party's future foreign policy and global standing.{{cite news|last=Bush|first=Stephen|author-link=Stephen Bush |url=http://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2015/08/andy-burnham-labour-should-have-woman-leader-when-time-right|title=Andy Burnham: Labour should have a woman leader "when the time is right" |work=New Statesman|date=25 August 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150828000302/http://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2015/08/andy-burnham-labour-should-have-woman-leader-when-time-right|archive-date=28 August 2015}}{{cite news|last=Mason |first= Rowena |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2015/aug/25/burnham-corbyn-nato-trident-labour |title=Burnham 'would resign from Corbyn cabinet' over Nato and Trident stance |date=25 August 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170328110034/https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2015/aug/25/burnham-corbyn-nato-trident-labour |archive-date=28 March 2017}} ====China==== Burnham has viewed [[China–United Kingdom relations|relations with China]] primarily through the lens of economic development. During a meeting with the Chinese consul Tang Rui in April 2026, Burnham supported closer cooperation "in areas such as green development, electric buses, advanced manufacturing and life sciences".{{Cite web |last=Wang |first=Orange |date=23 June 2026 |title=Will Andy Burnham shake up the UK's China policy if he becomes prime minister? |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3358096/will-andy-burnham-shake-uks-china-policy-if-he-becomes-prime-minister |access-date=4 July 2026 |website=[[South China Morning Post]] |language=en |archive-date=28 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260628233509/https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3358096/will-andy-burnham-shake-uks-china-policy-if-he-becomes-prime-minister |url-status=live }} ==== Russo-Ukrainian war ==== {{See also|United Kingdom and the Russo-Ukrainian war}} Burnham has supported [[Ukraine]] since the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]] amidst the wider [[Russo-Ukrainian war]], stating, "We must not allow Russia to prevail... In 2014, as the shadow health secretary, he condemned the [[2014 Russian annexation of Crimea]] and argued Russia should not be allowed to host the [[2018 FIFA World Cup]].{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-26679542|title=Fifa urged to rethink staging 2018 World Cup in Russia|website=[[BBC]]|date=21 March 2014|access-date=27 July 2026}} As Mayor of Greater Manchester, he practised this stance by establishing the Unbroken Cities Network alongside the [[Mayor of Lviv|mayors of Lviv]] and [[Mayor of Liverpool|Liverpool]] to support municipal recovery and rehabilitation programs for injured Ukrainians.{{Cite web |date=24 June 2026 |title=Amid UK political turmoil, Andy Burnham's rise offers reassurance to Ukraine |url=https://kyivindependent.com/will-britains-likely-next-prime-minister-change-course-on-ukraine/ |access-date=25 June 2026 |website=The Kyiv Independent |language=en |archive-date=24 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260624210159/https://kyivindependent.com/will-britains-likely-next-prime-minister-change-course-on-ukraine/ |url-status=live }} Upon succeeding Starmer as Prime Minister on 20 July 2026, Burnham immediately elevated his support to the state level. In one of his very first official actions on his first day in office, he held a phone call with Zelenskyy. During the conversation, Burnham explicitly reaffirmed that the UK's "steadfast and resolute" commitment to Ukraine would remain completely unchanged under his leadership, promising to stand with him "100%".{{Cite web |title=Zelenskyy holds first call with new UK PM and says meeting will follow |url=https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/07/20/8045026/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=Ukrainska Pravda |language=en}} ====Gaza war==== {{Main|United Kingdom and the Gaza war}} During the 2015 leadership campaign, Burnham pledged that his first overseas trip would be to Israel and joined Labour Friends of Israel.{{cite web |last1=Hawari |first1=Yara |title=Don't believe Andy Burnham's PR machine |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/amp/opinions/2026/7/20/dont-believe-andy-burnhams-pr-machine |website=[[Al Jazeera]] |date=20 July 2026 |access-date=22 July 2026}} However, following the outbreak of the [[Gaza war]] in October 2023, he became one of the first high-profile Labour figures to break ranks with then-leader Keir Starmer by publicly calling for a ceasefire.{{cite news |title=Labour divisions deepen over Gaza ceasefire stance |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-67238594 |access-date=27 June 2026 |work=[[BBC News Online]] |archive-date=1 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260701030258/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-67238594 |url-status=live }} While condemning the [[October 7 attacks]], Burnham cited profound concerns over civilian casualties and the humanitarian blockade. Andrew Murray Burnham (born 7 January 1970) is a British politician who has served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Leader of the Labour Party since July 2026. He has been Member of Parliament (MP) for Makerfield in Greater Manchester since June 2026, and was Mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to 2026; before that he was MP for Leigh from 2001 to 2017 and held several Cabinet positions. Burnham identifies as a socialist and is associated with the Labour Party's soft left; he is also a member of the Co-operative Party, which is allied with Labour. His political ideology has been called "Manchesterism". 
Burnham was born and brought up in northern England. He joined Labour at the age of 15 and read English at Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge. He worked as a journalist and political adviser before being elected the MP for Leigh in 2001. Under the prime ministers Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, he was Chief Secretary to the Treasury and Culture Secretary, in which capacity he launched the Hillsborough Independent Panel. In 2009 he was promoted to Health Secretary; he responded to the swine flu pandemic and launched an independent inquiry into the Stafford Hospital scandal.
After Labour's defeat at the 2010 general election, Burnham served in the shadow cabinet from 2010 to 2016. He stood for the Labour leadership in 2010 and in 2015, coming fourth and second respectively. In 2017 he stood down as an MP and was elected Mayor of Greater Manchester. He reorganised Manchester's tram and bus systems as the Bee Network and received the nickname "King of the North" for campaigning for more furlough funding for Northern communities during the COVID-19 pandemic. Burnham's tenure as mayor increased his national profile and he was re-elected in 2021 and in 2024.
Following Labour's return to government in 2024, Burnham maintained strong approval ratings as those of the prime minister, Keir Starmer, declined, and came to be seen as a potential successor. He returned to Parliament in 2026 by winning the Makerfield by-election and resigned as mayor. Starmer announced his resignation, leading to a party leadership election which Burnham won unopposed. During his premiership, Burnham has announced policies to move some government administration out of London as No. 10 North, cut fares on buses, reduce business rates on pubs, increase government support for apprenticeships, establish a National Care Service, and continue support for Ukraine.
